analysis.one_liner: Expands and extends federal compensation for people sickened by nuclear testing fallout and uranium mining.
analysis.headline: The House Judiciary Committee approved the bill 25–8 in December 2021, but it never received a House floor vote and died when the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill expands the Radiation Exposure Compensation Act, which pays people who got cancer after being exposed to radiation from Cold War nuclear weapons tests or from mining and milling uranium for the government's weapons program. It adds new affected areas (Colorado, Idaho, Montana, New Mexico, Guam, and more of Arizona, Nevada, and Utah), raises payments to $150,000, adds medical benefits, lets previously denied claimants try again, and extends the filing deadline and the compensation fund by 19 years. It also makes more uranium workers eligible for a separate federal program for nuclear-weapons workers and funds $3 million a year in university research on uranium mining's health effects on nearby communities.
analysis.who_benefits: Downwinders and uranium workers who were left out of the current program: residents of New Mexico near the 1945 Trinity test, people in newly added states, uranium miners, millers, core drillers, ore transporters, and mine remediation workers employed through 1990 (the current law cuts off at 1971), and their family members in affected communities. People previously denied compensation could resubmit up to three times, and people already paid could receive the difference up to the new $150,000 amount plus medical benefits [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Downwinders and uranium workers with cancer

how_it_helps.text: Adds Colorado, Idaho, Montana, New Mexico, Guam, and additional areas of Arizona, Nevada, and Utah to the areas whose residents can file claims, including people present near the Trinity test in New Mexico from 1944 onward [S2][S3].

Raises compensation for leukemia and specified cancers to a uniform $150,000 (from $50,000 or $75,000 under current law) and adds medical benefits on par with the program for nuclear-weapons facility workers [S2][S3].

Extends eligibility for uranium miners and millers through December 31, 1990 (current law ends at 1971), adds core drillers, ore transporters, and remediation workers, adds kidney cancers and chronic kidney disease to the covered illnesses, and lets workers combine years in different uranium jobs to qualify [S2][S3].

Extends the program's filing deadline and its funding by 19 years beyond enactment (current law terminates the program on July 10, 2022), lets denied claimants resubmit up to three times, and requires the Attorney General to accept affidavits and tribal records such as grazing permits and homesite leases as proof of presence or employment [S2][S3].

Creates a $3 million-a-year grant program through the National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences for universities to study uranium mining and milling's health effects on people who were not workers, including miners' families [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers, through the Radiation Exposure Compensation Trust Fund and the Energy Employees Occupational Illness Compensation Program, which would absorb the higher $150,000 awards, the 19-year extension, the added medical benefits, and new claimants from the added states and the post-1971 uranium workforce [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: The cost is real and open-ended: the bill roughly doubles or triples the per-claim award, extends the fund for 19 years, adds medical benefits that continue for life, and widens eligibility to a much larger pool of claimants — a significant new federal liability at a time when the existing program was scheduled to end in July 2022 [S2][S3].

A supporter would acknowledge that the bill pays a flat $150,000 based on where someone lived or worked rather than on a measured radiation dose, and that the expanded affidavit system eases the proof standards for employment and presence claims, which raises fair concerns about how claims are verified even though affidavits are sworn under penalty of perjury and must be corroborated [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The harms being compensated are well documented: downwinders near atmospheric nuclear tests and uranium workers developed cancers at elevated rates after exposure tied to the government's weapons program, and the current law was about to shut down with entire exposed regions still excluded. The cost is fiscal, concentrated in the federal treasury, and bounded by a 19-year sunset. The main design criticism is the flat award regardless of dose, but the tradeoff favors the people being compensated, who have no other route to redress for injuries the government's own program caused.

outcome.mechanism: The House Judiciary Committee voted 25–8 on December 8, 2021 to send the bill to the floor, but no floor vote was ever scheduled, and the bill expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Teresa Leger Fernandez introduced the bill on September 22, 2021 with 15 original cosponsors from both parties, including a New Mexico Republican [S1][S3].
It was referred to the Judiciary Committee and additionally to the Education and Labor and Energy and Commerce Committees, and then to the Energy Subcommittee [S5].
On December 8, 2021, the Judiciary Committee held a markup and voted 25–8, with 8 members opposed, to order the bill reported to the full House with amendments [S5].

The action record shows no further movement after that committee vote: the bill was never reported to the floor, never debated, and never voted on by the full House before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5][S1].
By the end, the bill had drawn 77 cosponsors — 67 Democrats and 10 Republicans — yet still never reached the floor [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The federal treasury avoided the added compensation costs, and the status quo held: people in the excluded regions and post-1971 uranium workers got no relief from this bill, even though a House committee had approved it with a strong bipartisan vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The federal treasury; the status quo held

industries.note: The bill compensates the industry's former workers for radiation-related illness, but the money comes from a federal fund, so the companies that employed them pay nothing and the legacy health costs stay on taxpayers. That public-pays arrangement continues unchanged.

industries.industry: Medical providers treating nuclear-weapons exposure victims
industries.note: The new medical benefits pay for treatment of compensated individuals through the same system used for nuclear-weapons facility workers, adding covered patients. Patients and their providers gain together.

The bill authorizes $3 million a year for fiscal 2022–2024 in grants to study uranium mining and milling's health effects on non-worker community members. The research funding follows the public-health interest.
